findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 99.7% of invoices paid within 30 days in both Q1 and Q2 2026/27, against a 99% target
findings.detail: The paper says both quarters were rated Green. It notes the KPI is a new measure (PI FS7a) that replaces the earlier 'invoices paid on time' indicator, and gives the 2025/26 outturn as 99.3%.
findings.matters: Prompt payment performance is a supplier-relations and payment-practice measure that finance teams at other councils track on the same basis.
findings.figures: 99.7% of invoices paid within 30 days (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); target 99%; 2025/26 outturn 99.3%
findings.quote: During the first six months of 2026/2027, data for this KPI has been reported as 99.7% of invoices paid on time for both Q1 and Q2, both quarters have been RAG rated Green, as they exceed the 99% target.

findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 58.49% of non-domestic rates collected in the first half of 2026/27, against an annual target of 98.81%
findings.detail: The paper states the half-year figure is on track to meet the target. For 2025/26 it reports an outturn of 99.12%, which it says met and exceeded target, against a national average of 96.8%.
findings.matters: Business rates collection drives retained income under the rates retention scheme, and the national comparison lets other finance teams benchmark performance.
findings.figures: 58.49% half-year collection (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); 2026/27 target 98.81%; 2025/26 outturn 99.12%; national average 96.8%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the half year (Q1 and Q2) percentage for non-domestic rates collected is 58.49% and is on track to meet the 98.81% target.

findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 58.67% of council tax collected in the first half of 2026/27, against an annual target of 99.19%
findings.detail: The paper states the half-year figure is on track to meet the target. It sets the 2025/26 annual outturn of 99.62% against a national average of 95.6%, and records that the 2025/26 target was met and rated Green.
findings.matters: Council tax collection is a core income line for a billing authority, and the paper gives a national average that peers and lenders can benchmark against.
findings.figures: 58.67% half-year collection (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); 2026/27 target 99.19%; 2025/26 outturn 99.62%; national average 95.6%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the half year (Q1 and Q2) percentage for Council tax collected is 58.67% and is on track to meet the 99.19% target.

findings.headline: Paragraph 2.3 gives the favourable net position as £423,064, while the table and paragraph 6.1 give £423,140.
findings.detail: The same discrepancy appears in income: paragraph 2.3 gives income £484,035 above profile, while the table gives £484,111. Paragraph 4.8 gives Recovered Rent Allowances as £25,431 favourable, while the summary of major variances gives £27,128.
findings.matters: Inconsistent headline figures in a monitoring report are something a finance director or a lender would want reconciled before relying on the numbers.
findings.figures: £423,064 (paragraph 2.3) vs £423,140 (table and paragraph 6.1); £484,035 vs £484,111 income; £25,431 vs £27,128 Recovered Rent Allowances
findings.quote: Both contribute to the favourable net position of £423,064.

findings.headline: Planning application and pre-application income is £43,237 favourable at half-year, a figure the paper says fluctuates with the timing of major developments.
findings.detail: The paper says income from planning applications varies month to month and depends on whether major developments are received within the financial period. It presents the current favourable position as subject to that variation.
findings.matters: Development-driven income is volatile for all planning authorities, and the paper's caveat shows why half-year variances on it may not hold to year-end.
findings.figures: £43,237 favourable (planning income)
findings.quote: The current position shows a favourable variance of £43,237.

findings.headline: Tipping charges invoiced late by Lancashire County Council give a £67,675 favourable variance, which the paper expects to clear once the charges are received.
findings.detail: The paper identifies delayed invoicing from LCC for tipping charges as a timing item. It expects the favourable variance to reverse when the invoices arrive.
findings.matters: Partner-invoice timing can make a half-year position look better than the year will end, which is relevant to anyone reading the headline underspend.
findings.figures: £67,675 favourable
findings.quote: It is expected that this variance will clear once the charges have been received.

findings.headline: £28,250 of earmarked reserves is being used to fund internal audit work by MIAA carried out in 2026/27 on the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.detail: The Resources Department is £29,164 adverse, and the paper says £28,250 of this will be met from earmarked reserves set aside for this purpose.
findings.matters: A finance director would note a reserve drawdown that funds audit costs for a prior year, which is the kind of call on reserves that lenders and peers track.
findings.figures: £28,250 from earmarked reserves; £29,164 Resources Department adverse
findings.quote: £28,250 is to be met from earmarked reserves in order to fund the internal audit work done by MIAA during 2026/27 in respect of the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.headline: The council has approved deleting two of the four works team posts and procuring an external contractor for two years for toilet cleaning, with Works Administration £45,909 adverse at half-year.
findings.detail: The paper says vacant posts produced lower staff costs, partly offset by temporary staff, and that the service has less oncost recharge income so far this year because of reduced productive staff time from vacancies and sickness absence.
findings.matters: The shift from in-house works and cleaning to external contractors is a service-delivery change that other councils are also weighing, and the paper shows its early income effect.
findings.figures: £45,909 adverse (Works Administration); two of four works team posts deleted; two-year contract
findings.quote: deletion of two of the four works team posts and to use outside external contractors

findings.headline: Albion Mill is £48,583 adverse, with three of five units vacant between April and July 2026 and renewal leases for the other two not yet agreed.
findings.detail: The paper says the budget assumed full occupancy and renewed leases at the start of the year. It attributes the delay to an ongoing lease consent issue and says new leases are hoped to be agreed in the coming months.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to see a property income shortfall tied to a lease consent problem that the paper describes as longstanding and unresolved.
findings.figures: £48,583 adverse (Albion Mill); £36,604 land rent shortfall; £11,205 non-domestic rates; £19,650 budgeted land rent income
findings.quote: Three of the five units at Albion Mill have been vacant between April and July 2026

findings.headline: Refuse Collection is £84,024 adverse at half-year, and refuse collection vehicle spend is £136,608 over budget.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the adverse position to temporary staff costs of £52,249 above profile and agency staff costs of £33,728 with no profiled provision. It says analysis of the overspend is underway with the service area.
findings.matters: Vehicle and agency costs in refuse collection are a common pressure across councils, and the paper shows the vehicle line as a separate and larger pressure than the staffing line.
findings.figures: £84,024 adverse (Refuse Collection); £136,608 over budget (vehicles); £52,249 temporary staff; £33,728 agency staff
findings.quote: Refuse Collection is £84,024 adverse.

findings.headline: Grant receipts were left out of the budget because of the timing of announcements, and the paper says the matching spend has not yet followed.
findings.detail: The paper says the net effect of grant receipt and consequential spend would be nil over the year, but that the timing of receipts and the absence of spend creates a favourable position. It proposes that the grants may be used for future spend, returned, or added to earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: Other councils receiving in-year grant announcements face the same timing mismatch, and the treatment of unspent grant at year-end affects reserves.
findings.figures: £459,187 combined grant underspend
findings.quote: There are various grant receipts not included in the budget due to the timing of announcements.

findings.headline: Health and Housing Committee shows a £446,424 favourable variance, larger than the council-wide favourable variance, and the other four committees together are £23,284 adverse.
findings.detail: The paper says the concentration is significant because the committee includes the Crisis and Resilience Fund, Renters Rights funding, Asylum Dispersal Grant and Homelessness funding.
findings.matters: A single committee carrying the whole favourable position shows how much of a council's half-year result can depend on grant income that sits outside its normal budget.
findings.figures: £446,424 favourable (Health and Housing); £23,284 adverse (other four committees combined); £277,417 Crisis and Resilience Fund
findings.quote: Health and Housing Committee has a favourable variance of £446,424, which is greater than the Council-wide favourable variance.

findings.headline: Excluding £459,187 of grants not yet spent, the half-year position is a net overspend of £36,047.
findings.detail: The paper adjusts the net position for the five grants it identifies, including the Crisis and Resilience Fund, Renters Rights, Building Safety Levy, Asylum Dispersal and Homelessness Grant. On that basis it reports an adjusted adverse variance of £36,047.
findings.matters: This is the figure the paper itself treats as the true half-year position, and it shows the council's underlying budget running adverse even before any year-end adjustment.
findings.figures: £459,187 grant underspend; £36,047 adjusted net overspend
findings.quote: Excluding these grants gives an adjusted adverse variance of £36,047.

findings.headline: At the half-year point the recorded net expenditure position is £423,140 below profiled budget, which the paper says is more than accounted for by £459,187 of grant funding whose spend has not yet been incurred.
findings.detail: The paper states that the favourable variance is more than accounted for by grant funding for which the associated expenditure has yet to be incurred. It also says the underspend should not be regarded as a saving or as a forecast of year-end outturn.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to know that a headline underspend at half-year is driven by grant timing rather than savings, since it can reverse as the grant spend follows.
findings.figures: £423,140 favourable against profile; £459,187 combined grant underspend
findings.quote: At the half-year point, the recorded net expenditure position is £423,140 below the profiled budget.

findings.headline: The authorised limit for external debt is set at £8,398k and the operational boundary at £2,566k for 2026/27, and the paper reports the council within both at September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper lists the prudential indicators for external debt and states that the council was within both limits for April to September 2026. It describes the authorised limit as the worst-case upper limit that cannot be breached without council approval.
findings.matters: These limits set the headroom for any future borrowing, so a lender or peer council can see the debt capacity the council has approved for 2026/27.
findings.figures: Authorised limit £8,398k; operational boundary £2,566k; within limits April to September 2026: YES

findings.headline: The council reports no long-term loan debt and no temporary loans taken out from April to September 2026, or in the same period of 2025.
findings.detail: The paper states that the council holds no long-term loan debt and that no short-term borrowing was needed in the period. It says its long-term borrowing policy is to use the PWLB where borrowing is required.
findings.matters: For a lender, a council with no external loan debt and no temporary borrowing in the period presents a different credit position from one with existing or rolling borrowing.
findings.figures: £0 long-term loan debt; no temporary loans in April to September 2026 or the same period of 2025
findings.quote: No temporary loans were taken out in the current financial year up to the 30th September

findings.headline: All of the council's deposits at 30 September 2026 were held with the Debt Management Office, totalling £24,950k of £25,030k invested.
findings.detail: The table of fixed-term deposits shows the Debt Management Office holding the whole of the fixed-term balance at 30 September 2026. The only other balance is £80k held with HSBC, the council's banking provider, which the paper adds to reach the £25,030k total.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere, or a lender assessing the council's cash counterparty exposure, would see that the entire deposit balance sat with the sovereign-backed DMO at that date.
findings.figures: £24,950k in fixed-term deposits with the DMO; £80k held with HSBC; £25,030k total invested; £22,500k invested at 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Fixed term deposits at 30 September 2026 0 24,950 0 24,950

findings.headline: The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its September 2026 meeting by a 6-3 vote, with three members voting for an increase to 4%.
findings.detail: The paper reports the September MPC decision and the vote split. It quotes the minutes saying UK CPI rose to 3.1% in August and is likely to rise further. The council states that higher energy-driven inflation has made a reduction in Bank Rate unlikely during 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council's investment income forecast depends on the rate it can earn on deposits, so a hold with an upward vote and no expected cut affects budget assumptions at any council that relies on short-term deposit income.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; vote 6-3; three members voting for a 0.25 percentage point rise to 4%; UK CPI 3.1% in August
findings.quote: Three members voted to increase the rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.

findings.headline: Interest on investments to 30 September 2026 was £429,436, against a budget of £393,990 to that date, and £527,961 in the same period of 2025.
findings.detail: The paper reports actual investment income for April to September 2026 against the budget for the same period, and against the same period in 2025. It says the 2025 returns were earned when interest rates were higher. The full-year budget is £787,980.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare this income-against-budget position with its own treasury returns, given that cash balances and rates have both moved.
findings.figures: £429,436 actual to end of September 2026; £393,990 budget to end of September; £787,980 full-year budget; variance -£35,446 as shown in the paper; £527,961 for the same period in 2025
findings.quote: which compares to £ 527,961 during the same period in 2025 when interest rates were higher.

findings.headline: Ribble Valley proposes to revisit its earlier decision not to charge council tax premiums on second homes and empty properties.
findings.detail: The Budget Working Group in July 2024 recommended against the new powers, citing no evidence that premiums reduce empty or second homes, avoidance routes, extra administration costs, and a possibly negligible benefit to the borough. The paper now proposes revisiting these considerations, including the administrative and recovery costs and the share of extra income the council would retain.
findings.matters: Reversing a prior policy position on premiums is a decision other councils facing similar gaps are weighing, and the retained-share and admin-cost questions decide whether it is worth doing.
findings.figures: £900K budget gap; 2028/29 earliest budget impact
findings.quote: It is proposed that the past considerations are revisited and further work be undertaken

findings.headline: Ribble Valley is reviewing options to help meet a £900K budget gap, including council tax discounts, premiums and exemptions, with any budget effect not until 2028/29.
findings.detail: The Budget Working Group discussed the wider options on 27 October 2026. The paper states that changes proposed at this stage would not affect the budget until 2028/29, because of the time needed for detailed assessment and possible consultation. The committee is asked to approve further work, with reporting back.
findings.matters: A stated budget gap with no closed funding solution, and a timetable that pushes any council tax measure two years out, is the kind of position a lender or peer finance officer would track.
findings.figures: £900K budget gap; budget impact not until 2028/29 financial year
findings.quote: review options to help meet the £900K budget gap

findings.headline: Ribble Valley's tax base grew 0.8% in 2026/27 and 0.91% in 2027/28, against a budgeted 1% per annum in its Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS budgets a 1% annual tax base increase. It reports the last two years at 0.8% and 0.91%, below that assumption. Over the ten years shown, the tax base rose from 22,902 in 2018/19 to 26,088 in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders can compare a council's tax base growth against its own budget assumption to judge whether council tax income is tracking the plan.
findings.quote: However, the last two years have seen increases of 0.8% and 0.91% respectively.

findings.headline: Ribble Valley's 2027/28 council tax base is 26,088 Band D equivalent, up 235 (0.91%) on 2026/27.
findings.detail: The tax base is calculated for all parishes and is the figure used to set Band D council tax for the billing authority, major precepting authorities and parish councils. Annex 1 shows the largest parish increases were Longridge (+117, 3.5%) and Clitheroe (+112, 1.8%).
findings.matters: The tax base is the denominator for every precepting body's Band D rate, so its growth sets how much council tax income each authority can raise before any rate change.
findings.figures: 26,088 tax base (Band D equivalent); increase of 235; 0.91%; 2026/27 tax base of 25,853
findings.quote: produces an overall tax base of 26,088 for 2027/28

findings.headline: The replacement ICT equipment for councillors scheme has not yet commenced, with completion expected by March 2027.
findings.detail: The scheme is rated amber. Engagement with councillors and the Corporate Management Team is the only task recorded, at 0% done.
findings.matters: A scheme with no spend and no started work six months into the year is one a finance officer will check against the rest of the capital programme's delivery.
findings.figures: £43,600 budget; £0 spent and committed; 0%; completion March 2027
findings.quote: This scheme has not yet commenced.

findings.headline: The regulatory services software upgrade's direct award to the supplier, due December 2025, is recorded as completed in September 2026, with commencement now expected in October 2026.
findings.detail: The scheme is rated amber, and the paper says the supplier was chosen partly to align with software used by other local councils in the context of local government reorganisation. Only 8% of the budget is spent or committed.
findings.matters: A milestone recorded roughly nine months after its due date, with the scheme not yet started, is the kind of slippage a finance director will want to see compared against their own software programmes.
findings.figures: £256,600 budget; £20,000 spent and committed; 8%; £236,600 remaining
findings.quote: this project is expected to commence in October 2026

findings.headline: The Council Offices mains upgrade is rated amber with 0% spent, and the paper says it requires a retender to allow for out-of-hours work.
findings.detail: The LED lighting element was completed in 2023/24. The power supply upgrade has been delayed because contractors pulled out, and the specification must be revised before a framework-based retender. Project management is planned after tendering.
findings.matters: A scheme that has been retendered after contractor withdrawal, with no spend yet, is a procurement risk other councils face when the market is thin for out-of-hours electrical work.
findings.figures: £96,840 budget after a -£1,480 move from 2025/26; £0 spent and committed; 0%; 3 green/amber schemes overall
findings.quote: but requires retender to allow for out of hours work

findings.headline: The network infrastructure scheme's proposed 24/7 cyber security managed service will be an additional revenue cost, the paper states.
findings.detail: Phase 1 firewall replacement is complete, and Phase 2 procurement is at 70% with the team still assessing frameworks. Phase 3 cyber security is at 20%, and the proposed managed service would add ongoing revenue spending on top of the capital budget.
findings.matters: A capital scheme that creates a recurring revenue cost is a budget-pressure point that finance directors and lenders will want to see priced into the medium-term plan.
findings.figures: Phase 1 complete; Phase 2 procurement 70%; Phase 3 20%; completion March 2027
findings.quote: but this will be an additional revenue cost.

findings.headline: The Revenues and Benefits replacement server is commissioned, with live data migration scheduled for 10 and 11 October 2026 and go-live planned for 12 October 2026.
findings.detail: Test data has been migrated to the new servers and internal testing is complete. The project's migration milestone is shown at 75% done, with the scheme expected to complete by November 2026.
findings.matters: Replacing a legacy platform on a dated schedule is a concrete delivery test, and the paper gives the cutover dates directly, so other councils can compare their own migration timelines.
findings.figures: £24,000 budget; £20,900 spent and committed; 87%; go-live 12 October 2026; completion November 2026
findings.quote: the new servers planned to go live on 12 October 2026

findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund and Rural England Prosperity Fund capital projects are reported complete at 30 September 2026, with 85% and 60% of budget spent or committed.
findings.detail: The paper says all projects under these capital schemes are complete, yet the table still shows remaining budgets of £35,169 for UKSPF and £18,156 for REPF. The final position is to be presented separately by the Director of Economic Development and Planning.
findings.matters: A scheme reported complete with unspent budget left is a reconciliation point a finance director will want to check against final outturn.
findings.figures: UKSPF: £242,538 budget, £207,369 spent and committed, 85%, £35,169 remaining; REPF: £45,426 budget, £27,270 spent and committed, 60%, £18,156 remaining
findings.quote: At this stage all projects under this capital scheme are now complete, as of the end of September.

findings.headline: The Ribble Valley Shared Prosperity Fund capital scheme had £305,491 spent or committed at 30 September 2026, 20% of the £1,544,928 budget slipped from 2025/26.
findings.detail: The budget is spread across 36 approved individual projects, with the remainder held as a single unallocated scheme. The paper says all projects are expected to complete in year.
findings.matters: A large slipped balance with 20% committed at mid-year is a concrete delivery test for the year, and the 36-project split shows how the council is managing it.
findings.figures: £1,544,928 slipped budget; £305,491 spent and committed; 20%; £1,239,437 remaining; 36 projects
findings.quote: At this stage all projects under this capital scheme are expected to be completed in year.

findings.headline: The main committee capital budget rose to £539,570 after £211,500 of 2025/26 slippage and a £67,700 additional approval by the Emergency Committee on 13 August 2026.
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 estimate was £260,370 including schemes moved from 2025/26. The paper says the £67,700 addition was for an existing scheme, approved at the Emergency Committee meeting of 13 August 2026.
findings.matters: Budget growth from slippage and mid-year approvals is a pattern other finance officers will recognise, and the size of the increase against the original estimate is visible in the paper's own table.
findings.figures: £260,370 original total; £211,500 slippage; £67,700 additional approval; £539,570 latest total
findings.quote: There was an additional budget approval of £67,700 made by the Emergency

findings.headline: Ribble Valley's six main committee capital schemes had £101,490 spent or committed at 30 September 2026, 18.8% of the £539,570 approved budget.
findings.detail: The paper reports three schemes rated green and three amber, with all six expected to complete within the financial year. The report also says the amber schemes will need continued close monitoring.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the 18.8% spend-to-date against their own in-year capital profile, and a lender can see how much of the programme is still uncommitted with six months of the year left.
findings.figures: £101,490 spent and committed; 18.8%; £539,570 approved budget; £438,080 remaining; 3 green, 3 amber
findings.quote: representing 18.8% of the approved budget of £539,570

findings.headline: Government confirmed a one-year delay to local government reorganisation, with vesting day in April 2029
findings.detail: The LGR Programme Manager reports a government pause in early September, and that RVBC continues to work with Lancaster and Preston on the proposed 'North' unitary council. On 29 October 2026 the government confirmed a one-year delay, moving the borough election to May 2027, shadow unitary elections to May 2028 and vesting day to April 2029.
findings.matters: The timetable for the council's transfer to a successor structure affects financial planning, budget horizons and the handover of finance functions for Ribble Valley and its neighbours.
findings.figures: one-year delay; borough election May 2027; shadow unitary council elections May 2028; vesting day April 2029; latest risk score 12 against target 4
findings.quote: 29 October 2026 – government confirmed a one-year delay meaning borough election in May 2027, shadow unitary council elections in May 2028 and vesting day in April 2029.

findings.headline: All service provision in Ribble Valley is being reviewed to bridge a £900K budget gap in 2027/28
findings.detail: The discretionary service provision risk (SRR005) was rescored, and the Director of Resources says all service areas are under review as part of the work to close the gap. The paper states this does not mean there is a direct risk to discretionary services. The gap is given against 2027/28, whereas the SRR002 update gives no year.
findings.matters: A council reviewing every service to close a stated gap is a pattern other finance officers and lenders will want to compare with their own savings programmes.
findings.figures: budget gap of £900K in 2027/28; latest risk score 9 (inherent 15, target 6)
findings.quote: All service provision is currently being reviewed as part of the work being undertaken to bridge the budget gap of £900K in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Ribble Valley says it needs to identify savings of approximately £900K, with a balanced budget not yet reached
findings.detail: The Director of Resources reports that the council must find around £900K of savings. Work on identifying savings has started, but the paper says much work is still to be done before a balanced budget is achieved. The affordable and sustainable budget risk (SRR002) has a latest residual score of 9 against a target of 6.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see the size of the unfunded gap and that no balanced position has yet been reached, as the council's own risk owner states it.
findings.figures: savings of approximately £900K; latest risk score 9; target risk score 6
findings.quote: At this point in time the council is in a position where it needs to identify savings of approximately £900K.

findings.headline: The paper gives the approved capital programme as £17,248,688 and the remaining budget as £8,071,933 in its conclusion, while its own tables show £17,238,694 and £8,061,939.
findings.detail: The section 4.1 figures differ from the Section 3.1 table and Annex 1 totals by £9,994 on both the programme and remaining budget. The spend figure of £9,176,755 is the same in both places.
findings.matters: A mismatch between a committee paper's conclusion and its own totals is the kind of reporting error a finance director would want to see corrected before the figures are relied on.
findings.quote: equivalent to 53% of the approved capital programme of £17,248,688 leaving £8,071,933 available.

findings.headline: Two schemes with £1,469,350 of budget are not expected to proceed in year, including the Longridge New 3G Pitch.
findings.detail: The paper rates two schemes black, Longridge New 3G Pitch and Fence and Gates Around Edisford Playing Pitches. Longridge has £25,018 spent or committed against a £1,415,580 budget, which is the largest single remaining budget on the black list.
findings.matters: A large pitch scheme deferred out of the year leaves most of its budget unspent at mid-year, which affects the council's reported in-year capital spend.
findings.figures: £1,469,350 combined budget; £25,018 spent or committed; £1,415,580 Longridge budget; 2 schemes
findings.quote: two are not expected to proceed in

findings.headline: The Joiners Arms refurbishment has had quotes rejected in favour of considering alternative buildings, including an empty Onward Homes site, with £4,754 of its £250,000 budget spent or committed.
findings.detail: The paper says quotes for renovation were received but the building's layout, age, size and accessibility limit the units. It says all options are being considered and that meetings have taken place with Onward Homes about an alternative site.
findings.matters: A council reconsidering an existing building against an alternative site is a change in project scope that a finance director at another council could compare with their own temporary accommodation plans.
findings.figures: £250,000 budget; £4,754 spent or committed; 2%
findings.quote: all options are being considered including alternative buildings to ensure best value for money

findings.headline: Three schemes with £325,900 of 2026/27 budget are unlikely to be completed within the financial year, including Joiners Arms Refurbishment and Temporary Housing.
findings.detail: The paper lists three red schemes: Temporary Housing, Joiners Arms Refurbishment and Drainage of Council Owned Football Pitches. For the football pitches, it says both sites cannot start because the ground is too hard, and that earlier work was held up by travellers on site at Mardale.
findings.matters: Schemes that cannot start because of ground conditions or site occupation show delivery risks that other councils running outdoor and housing capital works may also face.
findings.figures: 3 red schemes; £325,900 combined full-year budget; £54,400 football pitch drainage budget; £250,000 Joiners Arms budget; £21,500 Temporary Housing budget
findings.quote: three schemes are unlikely to be completed within the financial year

findings.headline: An affordable housing property purchase shows a £130,400 overspend against the Health and Housing budget, which the paper says will be resolved on discounted resale and financed from S106 monies.
findings.detail: The paper states the overspend is currently shown against the approved Health and Housing capital budgets. It says the gap between purchase price and discounted resale price will be met from S106 monies originally received for the affordable housing scheme.
findings.matters: Funding an overspend from S106 receipts and recovering it through a discounted resale is a specific mechanism a finance director could check against their own affordable housing purchases.
findings.figures: £130,400 spent against £0 budget; remaining budget -£130,400
findings.quote: currently showing as an overspend against the approved capital budgets within the Health and Housing

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool Refurbishment is at 92% of its £4,133,970 budget spent or committed and is rated green.
findings.detail: The Annex 1 line shows the scheme's original estimate, budget moved from 2025/26, slippage and additional approvals, giving a current budget of £4,133,970. The scheme has £332,396 remaining at 30 September 2026.

findings.detail: The report states that the potential income figures are for guidance only and are based on the 2026/27 base budget. It notes that service use may change in response to charge levels or market conditions, and that lower demand could reduce the amount achieved.
findings.matters: A fee uplift that depends on unchanged usage is a risk a lender or finance director will want to see stated, particularly where the income line is relied on to close a budget gap.

findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils can compare the uplift achieved against a central 3% assumption, and the gap between the target and the proposal shows how individual charge decisions move the total.

findings.matters: Councils and lenders in reorganisation areas need to know which bodies will set future budgets and over what horizon, and this report shows one authority extending its planning period.

findings.headline: Income from proposed fees is not guaranteed and will depend on service usage and demand, which may change in response to price increases
findings.detail: The report explicitly notes that the £1,902,435 projected income is based on activity assumptions for the review. Actual receipts will depend on service usage, which may change in response to revised charges. The council therefore cannot guarantee achieving the projected income levels even if the proposed fees are formally approved.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to understand revenue projections carry demand risk. If demand falls in response to fee increases, the council will fall further short on its budget target. This is material to any assessment of financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Projected income £1,902,435
findings.quote: The estimated income shown at Annex 1 illustrates the financial effect of the proposed charges using the activity assumptions adopted for this review. It is not a guaranteed level of income: actual receipts will depend on demand and service usage, which may change in response to the revised charges.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation pause extends budget-setting responsibility to at least 2028/29 and potentially beyond
findings.detail: The original Local Government Reorganisation timetable expected Ribble Valley to set its final budget in 2027/28. Following the reorganisation pause announced in September 2026, the council now expects to set budgets for at least 2028/29 and should plan on the assumption that it may remain responsible for balancing its budget beyond that date, pending government review and decisions.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director assessing the council's medium-term stability needs to know the timescale for any organisational change. This extends the period the council must balance its own books, moving target from 2027/28 to 2029/30, increasing financial risk.
findings.figures: LGR timeline originally 2027/28 as final budget; now at least 2028/29 and potentially beyond

findings.headline: Proposed fee increases generate approximately £8,000 above the baseline 3% forecast, within a £63,107 total increase
findings.detail: The fees review proposes charges that would increase budgeted income from £1,839,328 to £1,902,435. However, the medium-term forecast already factored in a 3% increase across the board; the additional 0.43% from these proposals represents only approximately £8,000 of new income. This shows how limited fees-based income solutions are against the scale of the budget gap.
findings.matters: Finance directors at other councils watching how peers respond to budget pressure need to understand whether fees are a viable lever for balancing. This shows fees alone cannot close a £0.9m deficit even with double-digit percentage rate increases.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budgeted income £1,839,328; 2027/28 projected income £1,902,435; total increase £63,107 (3.43%); additional income above forecast £8,000
findings.quote: As the medium-term forecast already assumes a 3% increase, only the additional 0.43%, approximately £8,000, represents an improvement against the forecast £0.9m budget gap for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Forecast budget gaps of £0.9m in 2027/28, £1.3m in 2028/29 and £2.7m in 2029/30 remain despite review of fees and charges
findings.detail: Although Ribble Valley set a balanced budget for 2026/27, significant budget gaps are forecast in the medium term, driven by reduction in government funding and loss of one-off transitional support after 2026/27. The proposed fees review will add only £8,000 above the already-forecast 3% income increase, making a minimal contribution to closing the 2027/28 gap. This means the council will need substantial savings or other funding actions to close these deficits.
findings.matters: A finance director assessing this council's financial trajectory and risk position needs to know whether the identified deficits have a funding solution. Forecast gaps of this scale extending three years, with limited progress from fees, signal a significant solvency risk.
findings.figures: £0.9m in 2027/28, £1.3m in 2028/29 and £2.7m in 2029/30; fees review adds only additional £8,000 above the forecast 3% baseline
findings.quote: Although the Council set a balanced budget for 2026/27, forecast budget gaps remain of £0.9m in 2027/28, £1.3m in 2028/29 and £2.7m in 2029/30.

findings.headline: Trade waste collections income is under pressure from businesses seeking bundled waste services, as the council does not yet offer food waste collection for commercial customers.
findings.detail: The council reports a decline in trade waste collection customers. Officers expect recovery once the council launches its food waste collection service later in the year.
findings.matters: A revenue service is losing customers to competitors due to a gap in the council's service offering. Recovery depends on the timing and uptake of the planned food waste launch.

findings.headline: Council has approved deletion of two of four Works Administration team posts and permanent outsourcing of toilet cleaning for two years.
findings.detail: As part of a Works Administration team review, the council will delete two of four works team posts and procure external contractors for repairs work; separately, will procure an external contractor permanently for two years to do toilet cleaning across the borough and delete internal toilet cleaner posts. findings.headline: Three senior Community Services posts are vacant with recruitment on hold pending Local Government Reorganisation decision.
findings.detail: Head of Engineering Services, Engineering Services Manager, and Refuse and Workshop Manager posts are vacant. Recruitment is being held while future management requirements are reconsidered ahead of LGR. Vacancies create staff cost underspends (£46,539 to date) but are being partially offset by external consultants and temporary acting-up arrangements. The paper explicitly states that much of the salary underspend is being used to fund external consultant costs, so the underspend will not remain favorable. Vacancy also reduces charges to capital programme.
findings.matters: Management vacancies create strategic and operational risk and usually drive reliance on consultants at premium cost. The decision to hold recruitment due to LGR uncertainty is understandable but sustains ambiguity about post-LGR structure and staffing needs.
findings.figures: Three senior posts vacant; Salary underspend £38,477 to end August (due to these vacancies); LGR timing uncertain
findings.quote: The recruitment for these vacant posts is currently on hold, whilst the future management requirements for the Engineering Services and Depot sections in the run up to LGR are considered. In the meantime, some staff are temporarily acting up to help cover these vacancies and the Council has engaged external input to help with project management and contract administration on the Council's capital schemes. Much of this underspend is being used to fund the work of external consultants, so will not remain as a favourable variance.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool is closed April–November 2026 for refurbishment, eroding income across car parks, course fees, and leisure activity.
findings.detail: Pool closure is reducing car park income at Edisford by at least £10,621 (loss of visits). Planned swimming lessons income has not materialized: £7,840 of budgeted summer holiday lessons were cancelled when the external venue became unavailable, and evening lessons at the external facility are taking less uptake than budgeted. The pool course income variance to end August is £12,358 unfavorable. Offsetting benefit: pool staff redeployed to grounds maintenance reduced temporary staffing costs elsewhere. Income budgets will be reviewed at revised estimate stage.
findings.matters: Loss of a major leisure facility for eight months is operational disruption in a demand-led income service. The council faces income headwind for the duration, then must forecast recovery post-reopening, which depends on take-up returning to baseline.
findings.figures: Pool closure April–November 2026; Edisford car park income down £10,621; Pool course income under-recovery £12,358 to end August

findings.headline: Vehicle fleet repairs costs are elevated by necessity to hire replacement vehicles and third-party contractor cover during a Vehicle Mechanic vacancy, but council has now recruited to the post.
findings.detail: Refuse collection vehicle repairs and maintenance overspend £72,698 to end August, driven by costs of hiring replacement vehicles while council vehicles are being repaired, third-party workshop cover during the mechanic vacancy, and external technician input for specific repairs. The paper notes that recruitment difficulties to the mechanic post have contributed to more expensive repairs downstream and greater outsourcing. A new Vehicle Mechanic has been recruited and will start shortly; the Apprentice Mechanic post will then be advertised. These recruitment completions should reduce external labor costs.
findings.matters: The mechanism of the overspend—needing to hire vehicles while repairs are delayed and then pay for external labor—is a sign either of fleet age, utilization intensity, or both. Once recruitment completes, this should improve, but the underlying position (why repairs take so long, why the fleet requires such cost-intensive intervention) remains unclear.
findings.figures: Vehicle repairs overspend £72,698 to end August; Vehicle Mechanic vacant since start of 2026/27; new Vehicle Mechanic recruited, start date imminent
findings.quote: It is mainly due to the costs of hiring vehicles whilst repairs are being carried out on Council owned vehicles, workshop cover from a third-party contractor whilst there is a vacancy for a Vehicle Mechanic and procuring external vehicle technician input for some issues.

findings.headline: Diesel costs are 27% higher than budgeted across the refuse vehicle fleet, with unit price inflation accounting for approximately 25% of the variance.
findings.detail: Diesel spend to end August is £25,215 over budget. The paper identifies that actual diesel per-unit rates are approximately 25% higher than estimated when the budget was set, though some additional variance may reflect utilization. This variance is across the council's refuse fleet specifically, but points to broader fuel inflation pressure. Officers are exploring alternative fuels including HVO.
findings.matters: Fuel cost inflation is a structural pressure for waste collection services. If sustained, this requires permanent budget uplift, not one-off management action.
findings.figures: Diesel spend 27% higher than budgeted to end August; Unit rates 25% higher than estimate; Overspend £25,215 to end August
findings.quote: Diesel spend across all the Council's refuse vehicles was 27% higher than budgeted for to date. This was due to the diesel per unit rates being approximately 25% higher than estimated when the budget was set.

findings.headline: Refuse collection and vehicles show £170,080 combined overspend to end August, concentrated in temporary staffing, agency cover, and fleet maintenance.
findings.detail: Refuse collection services overspend £84,192, including £43,563 on temporary staff and £29,665 on agency drivers covering two vacant posts. Vehicle repairs and maintenance overspend £72,698, mainly from hiring replacement vehicles during repairs and third-party contractor cover while a Vehicle Mechanic post remains vacant. Diesel costs £25,215 over budget. Finance and operations are analyzing whether increased staffing costs reflect permanent demand changes.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a statutory demand-led service and represents the largest single budget item (£1.9m). If the staffing overspend is structural, it requires baseline correction rather than one-off management.
findings.figures: Refuse Collection overspend £84,192; Vehicle repairs and maintenance overspend £72,698; Diesel overspend £25,215; Vehicle Mechanic post vacant since April 2026
findings.quote: There has been a substantially higher level of use of temporary staff in-year so far than the original estimate budget allowed for. There has also been use of agency drivers to cover staffing shortfalls whilst two posts were vacant and to ensure rounds were completed and the department was on schedule with collections.

findings.headline: Core finance functions have ongoing staffing vacancies, with internal audit outsourcing planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: The Resources Department experienced a salary underspend of £84,213 primarily due to vacancies in Accounts, ICT and Audit sections. The council is setting aside £80,000 of this underspend in earmarked reserves to cover service continuity costs in 2026/27, specifically for internal audit services following planned outsourcing of the internal audit function. This indicates both ongoing staffing pressures and a structural change to governance functions.
findings.matters: Vacancies in core financial and audit functions, coupled with outsourcing of internal audit, weaken governance capacity and control oversight. This is significant during Local Government Reorganisation, which may compound organizational transition risks.
findings.figures: £84,213 salary underspend; £80k set aside in earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Mainly due to vacancies within the Accounts, Audit and ICT sections. £80k of the underspend has been set aside in earmarked reserves to support continuity of these services during the 2026/27 financial year, including outsourcing of the Internal Audit service.

findings.headline: EPR funding of £791,804 per annum may need adjustment as packaging volumes and scheme develop
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £791,804 EPR income annually (approximately £792k) and has assumed this continues in future years. However, the report warns: 'While Government has provided assurances around the scheme, the longer-term value remains a risk as packaging volumes and the scheme itself develop. The level of income allowed for in the forecast may need to be adjusted as further information becomes known.' This is a material income stream (4.4% of general fund) that may be unstable.
findings.matters: EPR is a new, developing scheme and the council is already factoring it into recurring budget assumptions. Loss or reduction of this income would force additional budget rebalancing in years when the £0.895m gap is already unaddressed.
findings.figures: 2026/27 EPR income: £791,804 (assumed recurring in future years)
findings.quote: While Government has provided assurances around the scheme, the longer-term value remains a risk as packaging volumes and the scheme itself develop.

findings.headline: Potential external borrowing needed if capital spending and LGR costs deplete cash faster than expected
findings.detail: The council currently has no external debt and has used internal resources (reserves) to finance its capital programme. However: 'If cash balances reduce more quickly than expected, external borrowing may be needed, which would impact the revenue forecast.' The approved four-year capital programme is £16.962m (£12.860m in 2026/27 alone), financed by reserves and balances. The report suggests that the council should 'review existing schemes for deliverability, affordability and relevance' rather than invite new bids, signalling concern about cash adequacy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can finance its capital programme without recourse to borrowing. The report's language ('may be needed') indicates this is uncertain and could tip from possibility to necessity quickly. Any external borrowing will add revenue costs at a time when the revenue budget is already in deficit.
findings.figures: Capital programme 2026/27–2029/30: £16.962m; £12.860m in 2026/27; £1.322m internal borrowing assumed 2026/27
findings.quote: If cash balances reduce more quickly than expected, external borrowing may be needed, which would impact the revenue forecast.

findings.headline: First-quarter 2026/27 overspend of £129k suggests the current year may not balance unless corrected
findings.detail: As of end-June 2026, the council shows a net adverse variance of £129,249 (4.27%) against the original budget. Key drivers: Housing Benefits £423k adverse, Trade Waste income £32k adverse (described as 'likely to be the outturn position unless new contracts are secured'), planning appeals consultant costs £38k adverse. If this variance runs pro-rata for the full year, the 2026/27 outturn overspend would be approximately £516k, far exceeding the £277k planned drawdown from balances.
findings.matters: A first-quarter variance this large, driven in part by structural income shortfalls (Trade Waste) rather than one-off items, raises questions about budget realism. If 2026/27 closes with a material unplanned overspend, reserves will be drawn down faster than forecast, worsening the cash position ahead of 2027/28.
findings.figures: Q1 net variance: £129,249 (4.27%); Housing Benefits adverse £423k; Trade Waste adverse £32k; planning appeals adverse £38k
findings.quote: For the first quarter, there shows a net overspend/under recovery of income of £129,249. Positive amounts are adverse and negative amounts are favourable unless otherwise stated.

findings.headline: Interest income falling from £788k to £440k despite current Bank Rate of 3.75%, driven by capital-spending and LGR depletion of cash
findings.detail: The council previously benefited from higher investment income. Even though Bank Rate sits at 3.75%, the forecast income is dropping sharply: from £787,980 in 2026/27 to £440,000 in 2027/28 (a £348k hit in one year). The reason: 'Due to heavy investment through the capital programme, largely funded by the Council's earmarked reserves and general fund balances, this substantially reduces the monies available for investment.' This signals that the council's cash buffer is being rapidly consumed by capital spending and LGR costs.
findings.matters: Interest income does not solve any budget problem; it merely masks the underlying deficit. A council burning reserves to fund capital while facing a structural revenue gap is on an unsustainable path. The drop in available cash is a leading indicator of reserve depletion.
findings.quote: Due to heavy investment through the capital programme, largely funded by the Council's earmarked reserves and general fund balances, this substantially reduces the monies available for investment.

findings.headline: LGR (merger with Preston and Lancaster from April 2028) creates unquantified costs beyond the £487k already budgeted
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £487,571 for LGR contribution to the Lancashire Transition Fund. However, the report explicitly states: 'The MTFS published in March 2026 recognises that further costs are likely but, because they could not then be quantified, no additional provision was included.' Unquantified risks include management/finance capacity, dual-running costs, systems migration, contract terminations, and the possibility of expenditure becoming redundant before vesting day. Officer capacity will be diverted, reducing ability to deliver savings or capital projects.
findings.matters: Unknown LGR costs in a year when the budget already has a £0.895m gap suggests the true budget pressure is worse than reported. The report warns that 'decisions which commit the successor authority to significant new expenditure will require particularly careful consideration', signalling that financial discipline is weakening precisely when it should tighten.
findings.figures: £487,571 budgeted; further costs 'likely but...could not then be quantified'
findings.quote: The MTFS published in March 2026 recognises that further costs are likely but, because they could not then be quantified, no additional provision was included.

findings.headline: Business-rates reset ends historic growth income; the council no longer pools and baseline uncertainty remains
findings.detail: Ribble Valley historically benefited significantly from business-rate growth and Lancashire pooling gains. The 2026 reset fixed a new baseline and introduced a levy on growth; the council chose not to pool in 2026/27 and pooling for the single year before LGR looks 'unlikely'. Growth is now subject to levy charges. Separately, government will retrospectively adjust 2026/27 baselines in the 2027/28 settlement based on summer 2026 data collection—the council does not know if this adjustment will be favourable or adverse.
findings.matters: The reset removes a revenue stream the council relied on historically. Growth is now constrained by levy design and uncertain due to a pending retrospective revaluation. For a lender, this signals permanent loss of income resilience—the council cannot grow its way out of budget pressures as it could before.
findings.figures: Safety net reduced from 100% to 97% (2027/28) then 92.5% (2028/29); no pooling gains protection from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: The Council had previously benefited significantly from locally generated business rate growth and from membership of the Lancashire Business Rates Pool. The full reset of business rates baselines from 1 April 2026 is a fundamental change.

findings.headline: £466k Adjustment Support Grant expires after 2026/27, creating a 'cliff edge' in government funding
findings.detail: This one-off payment was granted as transitional protection in 2026/27 only, relating to the treatment of historic business-rate pooling gains. It provides no recurring revenue stream. The council explicitly identifies this as creating 'a particularly important cliff edge for the 2027/28 budget', yet the budget gap of £0.895m is only slightly smaller than the grant itself, suggesting little mitigation planned.
findings.matters: A £466k funding cliff is structural and timing-certain. It forces budget rebalancing in a year when other pressures (LGR, pay inflation, capital spending) are already rising. The council acknowledges the risk but has not pre-funded it.
findings.figures: £466k (one-off payment in 2026/27 only); net 2027/28 gap £0.895m
findings.quote: This was a one-off payment for 2026/27 only and the full impact of these changes will therefore be felt from 2027/28 onwards. This creates a particularly important 'cliff edge' for the 2027/28 budget.

findings.headline: Budget gap of £0.895m in 2027/28 requires active mitigation but has no agreed funding solution
findings.detail: The council moves from a balanced 2026/27 budget to a forecast gap of £0.895m for 2027/28, rising to £1.313m in 2028/29. The report identifies this as a 'known budget issue that needs to be addressed' but offers no concrete savings plan, relying instead on generic guidance to service committees to identify pressures and savings during budget preparation.
findings.matters: A £0.895m recurring gap that has not been funded is the definition of unsustainable budget planning. Lenders assess whether a council can balance its books; unaddressed multi-year gaps suggest either service cuts or reserves drawdown ahead.
findings.quote: the latest forecast gap of £0.895m in 2027/28 needs to be actively addressed, as our funding is reasonably certain compared to past years during the September forecast.

findings.headline: Business rates collection position swung from £441K surplus to £191K deficit
findings.detail: The business rates element of the collection fund deteriorated materially, moving from an opening surplus of £441K to a closing deficit of £191K—a swing of £632K. Meanwhile council tax collection also deteriorated from a £915K surplus to £424K. Overall, the collection fund surplus fell from £1.356m to £233K, a reduction of 83%.
findings.matters: A deteriorating collection fund position, particularly the shift to business rates deficit, signals underlying weakness in commercial property valuation or collection in the area. This affects cash flow and suggests economic headwinds.
findings.figures: Collection fund overall: opened £1.356m surplus, closed £233K surplus; business rates: opened £441K surplus, closed £191K deficit; council tax: opened £915K surplus, closed £424K surplus
findings.quote: The overall opening balance on the collection fund at 1 April 2025 was an overall surplus of £1.356m. The overall closing balance at 31 March 2026 was a surplus of £233K.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates cost pressures and structural uncertainty
findings.detail: The council has set aside £200K for LGR costs in 2025/26, plus £14K for staff training to prepare for reorganisation. The report explicitly flags ongoing uncertainty over funding, service costs and the implications of reorganisation, and notes that balances should not be relied upon to address future risks.
findings.matters: LGR represents structural change with uncertain outcomes and costs. A lender would need to understand how the reorganisation affects the council's future financial position, borrowing needs, and tax base.
findings.figures: £200K set aside for LGR costs in 2025/26; £14K for staff training in preparation for LGR
findings.quote: The Council continues to face uncertainty over future funding, service costs and the implications of local government reorganisation. The availability of balances does not remove the need to maintain sustainable ongoing revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves will be depleted by 61% to finance capital schemes; £9.6m drawn in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council has committed £11.9m of its £16.591m earmarked reserves to capital schemes over the next four years, with £9.553m scheduled for drawdown in 2026/27. By 31 March 2027, earmarked reserves will fall to £6.505m. The council notes that what remains is substantially committed to specific schemes and capital financing, leaving minimal general flexibility.
findings.matters: The council is funding a substantial capital programme almost entirely from accumulated reserves rather than borrowing. This strategy depletes financial buffers and raises questions about how future capital investment will be financed.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves at 31 March 2026: £16.591m; capital programme total 2026/27–2029/30: £11.9m; 2026/27 drawdown: £9.553m; forecast balance at 31 March 2027: £6.505m
findings.quote: The capital programme shows that £11.9m of earmarked reserves will be used to finance schemes from 2026/27 to 2029/30. In 2026/27 £9.553m of this is expected to be used.

findings.headline: General fund balances will fall by 55% in 2026/27, dropping to £2.1m after drawing £2.29m for capital
findings.detail: The council is depleting general fund balances significantly to finance 2026/27 capital spending. Starting from £4.651m on 1 April 2026, the council will draw £2.29m for capital and forecasts an operating deficit of £277.7K, leaving only £2.084m in unallocated general fund balance by 31 March 2027. This reduces financial flexibility and resilience substantially.
findings.matters: A lender assessing resilience would be concerned that the council is reducing its financial buffer to below £2.1m when it faces ongoing uncertainty over funding and the costs of local government reorganisation.
findings.figures: Balance at 31 March 2026: £4.651m; drawn for 2026/27 capital: £2.290m; forecast balance at 31 March 2027: £2.084m
findings.quote: Members should note that £2.29m of the General Fund Balances position at 31 March 2026 is to be used to finance the capital programme during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Professional debt recovery charges incurred on rates and council tax
findings.detail: The council has incurred £5,897 in professional legal charges for debt recovery on business rates and council tax in the first four months. The council states these costs will be recovered from debtors where collection succeeds.
findings.matters: Use of professional recovery suggests either elevated arrears or active collection enforcement; either indicates potential cash flow friction and cost to recover sums owed.
findings.figures: £5,897 recovery charges through July
findings.quote: Professional debt-recovery charges have been incurred during the period in respect of business rates and council tax debt. These costs will be recovered from debtors where recovery is successful.

findings.headline: Restructuring reserve drawn down at 3x planned rate
findings.detail: The Restructuring Reserve is being depleted at £48,005 through July, against a budgeted draw of £11,880—more than triple the planned spend. This acceleration is driven by Local Government Reorganisation staffing and equipment costs arriving earlier and faster than anticipated.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown above plan reduces financial flexibility mid-year; if LGR costs continue at this rate, the reserve could exhaust well before the financial year closes, forcing difficult rebalancing decisions.
findings.figures: £48,005 actual spend vs £11,880 budgeted through July
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation staffing costs incurred during the period to July. The expenditure was approved by this committee in March 2026, and is to be funded from underspends on other budget areas.

findings.headline: Internal audit function outsourced after recruitment vacancies; £26,125 overspend funded from earmarked reserves through July
findings.detail: The council outsourced its mandatory internal audit function after failing to recruit to vacant posts. Through July the outsourced service has cost £120,985 against a £94,860 budget—a £26,125 overspend being funded from earmarked reserves specifically set aside for this purpose.
findings.matters: Outsourcing a core assurance function at premium cost signals either capacity constraints or labour market challenges; funding it from reserves rather than finding offsetting savings reduces financial buffer.
findings.figures: £26,125 overspend; budget £94,860, actual £120,985 through July
findings.quote: The mandatory internal audit service was outsourced following unsuccessful recruitment into several vacant posts (approved by this Committee in March 2026). The cost of audit work procured during the period has exceeded the budget that was established from the vacant posts.

findings.headline: Land charges search income down 43% as housing market slows
findings.detail: Income from property searches is running at £11,882 against a £20,908 budget through July. The council attributes this to lower search volumes caused by higher mortgage costs and market uncertainty. If the current run-rate continues, the annual shortfall could reach £27,000 on a full-year budget of £64,270.
findings.matters: A material decline in discretionary income during a slowdown squeezes cash and reduces flexibility; councils typically cannot quickly replace this revenue and must either cut services or draw reserves.
findings.figures: £11,882 actual vs £20,908 budgeted through July; full-year budget £64,270
findings.quote: Income from searches of the Land Register is lower than in previous years, reflecting lower search volumes. The housing market has slowed this year due to higher mortgage costs and future uncertainty.

findings.headline: Investment income fell 22% year-on-year to £1.09m as interest rates decline, reducing self-financing capacity.
findings.detail: Interest received on temporary investments and cash balances fell from £1,394,303 (2024/25) to £1,092,804 (2025/26), a decline of £301,499. This reflects the Bank of England base rate cut from 4.50% to 3.75% during the year and falling average investment rates from 4.88% to 4.00%. The council exceeded its revised estimate by £14.8k but faces structural headwinds as rates are forecast to fall further.
findings.matters: Declining interest income materially reduces the council's ability to self-finance capital or operational pressures from surplus cash, potentially forcing reliance on council tax growth, government grants, or reserves.
findings.quote: The average interest rate per investment placed was 4.00% during the 2025/26 financial year compared to 4.88% during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Council is depleting investment balances rather than borrowing to fund capital, with liquidity down £1.02m year-on-year.
findings.detail: Despite capital spending of £3.9m in 2025/26, the council did not borrow from PWLB or undertake temporary loans, instead drawing down its investment holdings from £24.78m (31 March 2025) to £23.76m (31 March 2026). The council retains PWLB access but has chosen to self-fund from reserves, with funds held in low-risk DMO investments (£22.5m) and HSBC (£1.26m).
findings.matters: Depleting investment balances to fund capital works reduces liquidity headroom and may limit the council's capacity to absorb financial shocks or maintain reserves if capital spending accelerates or income declines further.
findings.figures: Total investments: £23.76m (31 March 2026) vs £24.78m (31 March 2025); Year-on-year decline: £1.02m; PWLB borrowing: £0
findings.quote: All long-term debt that was held with the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) was repaid during the 2022/23 financial year and there were no long-term borrowing requirements during the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 49% of revised estimate, with £3.45m of planned spending slipped to 2026/27.
findings.detail: Original capital forecast of £13.94m was reduced to £6.87m at revised estimate during the year. Actual expenditure was £3.42m (core programme) or £3.90m including UKSPF schemes, representing £3.45m less than the revised budget. Community Services achieved only £0.83m of a £8.67m forecast, and Health and Housing £2.22m of a £3.16m forecast. The council attributes the shortfall to project slippage.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to deliver planned capital spending may indicate project delivery challenges, financial constraint, or scope changes that affect the council's service investment trajectory and long-term resilience.
findings.figures: Original forecast: £13.94m; Revised estimate: £6.87m; Actual: £3.42m; Variance: £3.45m below revised
findings.quote: Actual expenditure was £3.45m below the revised estimate , mainly due  to slippage on several schemes into the 202 6/27 capital programme.

findings.headline: Council becomes liable for £11,205 in NNDR charges on vacant Albion Mill units as landlord
findings.detail: Units 1, 2 and 3 at Albion Mill became vacant April-July 2026, creating an unexpected NNDR liability for the council as landlord. The £11,205 figure represents a full-year NNDR charge for the units (will reduce if units are re-let in-year). Additional costs from the vacant period (gas, electricity, service charges, solicitors' fees) are not yet fully charged to the council.
findings.matters: This is an unbudgeted cost arising from failure of occupancy assumptions, adding to the financial pressure from the Albion Mill income shortfall.
findings.figures: £11,205 NNDR liability (representing full-year charge)
findings.quote: The Council, as landlord, is liable for the NNDR on any units that become vacant in-year. Units 1, 2 and 3 have been vacant between April and July 2026, meaning there is a NNDR liability for the Council in-year.

findings.headline: Albion Mill property income shortfall of £26,779 due to vacancies and consent issues blocking lease renewals
findings.detail: Three of five units at Albion Mill have been vacant April-July 2026 and renewal leases for the other two units (at increased rent levels) have not been agreed, both unforeseen at budget time when full occupancy was assumed. The blockage stems from a lease consent disagreement with the underlessor that has only now been verbally resolved (August 2026) but not yet formalised. The £26,779 under-recovery also includes £20,542 in former tenant arrears from previous years (one tenant owes £20,193), which have proven difficult to collect.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can generate the income it forecasts from its property holdings. This shows mid-year failure of core budget assumptions and collection difficulties on a material revenue stream.
findings.figures: £26,779 total under-recovery; £6,237 Q1 2026/27 under-recovery from rent; £20,542 in arrears from prior years (one tenant £20,193)
findings.quote: Three of the five units at Albion Mill have been vacant between April and July 2026 and renewal leases for the other two units at increased rent levels had not been agreed. None of this was estimated in the original estimate budget, which was set on the basis of full occupancy.

findings.headline: Over £360k in grant funding received but not yet spent may force a reserve drawdown if not expended in year.
findings.detail: The council received Crisis and Resilience Fund grant (£167,210), Renters Rights Act S31 grant (£60,000), Heating Oil CRF grant (£97,266), Asylum Dispersal Scheme grant (£37,200), and Adult Social Care Transformation funding (£12,803), totalling well over £360k. None of this had been anticipated in the Original Estimate. The paper states: "If not spent in year, this funding would need to be set aside in earmarked reserves for spend at a future date." This is a cash management risk.
findings.matters: Grant-funded spend that carries forward creates a reserve liability. If the council cannot spend this funding in-year, it creates a commitment that reduces future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Crisis & Resilience Fund grant income £167,210; Renters Rights Act grant £60,000; Heating Oil grant £97,266; Asylum Dispersal grant £37,200; Adult Social Care Transformation £12,803
findings.quote: If not spent in year, this funding would need to be set aside in earmarked reserves for spend at a future date.

findings.headline: Environmental Health externally sources statutory inspection work because the council has no qualified staff, and this overspend will repeat.
findings.detail: The council has zero budgeted for Environmental Health Consultants but has already spent £7,150 by end July. The paper states this is "Over budget as in previous years as the Council have no suitably qualified member of staff to carry out certain inspections which are part of its statutory duty." The action plan is to "Bring in budget at Revised Estimate" — meaning this is expected to continue. Flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: A council unable to resource statutory functions internally faces recurring budget pressure and potential service risk. This is a structural problem, not a one-off variance.
findings.figures: Budgeted £0; actual £7,150 to end July; variance £7,150 overspend
findings.quote: Over budget as in previous years as the Council have no suitably qualified member of staff to carry out certain inspections which are part of its statutory duty.

findings.headline: Clitheroe Market maintenance is running 83% over budget four months in and is unlikely to recover.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £9,880 for annual repairs and maintenance of Clitheroe Market. By end July, £11,623 has been spent. The paper flags specific costs: £5k on a new roof for a market cabin, £760 on relaying unstable flags, and £2,340 on fire doors. The paper explicitly states "This expense area is already far exceeding budget early in the financial year. It is unlikely to recover the overspend as the year progresses." Flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance running over budget suggests either deferred maintenance or an asset in poor condition. Either way, this indicates future capital or revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Budgeted £9,880 for full year; actual £11,623 to end July; variance £7,531 overspend
findings.quote: This is a reactive area of expensive with repairs being carried out as necessary. In the first part of 2026/27 a large amount (£5k) has been spent on a new roof for one of the market cabins, plus £760 on relaying unstable flags and £2,340 on fire doors.

findings.headline: Affordable rental housing is delivering no income four months in, due to delays in preparing properties and leases.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £17,270 of rental income from affordable rent properties in 2026/27. By end July, only £801 has been received. The paper attributes this to "longer than expected time taken in preparing the properties and leases"; repair works have now been completed and leases progressed with Onward Homes. The £7,835 shortfall is flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director assesses council balance sheets on asset productivity. Budgeted income from council-owned rental properties is not being realised, indicating either an optimistic budget or a problem with asset handover.
findings.figures: Budget £17,270 for full year; actual £801 to end July; variance £7,835 overspend
findings.quote: The longer than expected time taken in preparing the properties and leases means that an amount of the rental income budgeted for in 2026/27 will not be achieved.

findings.headline: Joiners Arms renovation abandoned; council considering alternative site due to building constraints.
findings.detail: The Joiners Arms Refurbishment scheme received quotes for renovation but these revealed the "location layout, and age of the building limits the size and accessibility of the units." The council is now considering alternative buildings entirely, with discussions underway with Onward Homes on a different site. Only £4,754 (1.9%) of the £250k budget has been committed.
findings.matters: Mid-delivery scope reversal and site changes suggest planning deficiencies in the original scheme design, indicating possible project management or capacity issues.
findings.figures: JARFB: £250,000 budget, £4,754 spent (1.9%), now considering alternative site
findings.quote: the location layout, and age of the building limits the size and accessibility of the units. Therefore, all options are being considered including alternative buildings

findings.headline: Purchase of Affordable Housing budget of £500k spent to only £26 with no committed schemes.
findings.detail: This scheme has spent just £26 of its £500k approved budget by end July. The monitoring report notes: "Options for spend are still being considered. Schemes with specific time restrictions have been prioritised." No specific affordable housing purchase has been identified or committed.
findings.matters: Undeployed budget for a core council service (affordable housing) at year mid-point raises questions about affordable housing delivery capacity and whether budgets reflect realistic delivery plans.
findings.figures: PAHSG: £500,000 approved budget, £26 spent (0.0%), £499,974 remaining
findings.quote: Options for spend are still being considered. Schemes with specific time restrictions have been prioritised.

findings.headline: Cemetery Extension faces High environmental risk requiring permit and multiple outstanding assessments.
findings.detail: The Tier 2 groundwater assessment identified a HIGH environmental risk score and concluded an environmental permit will be required. As of late July 2026, quotations for Biodiversity Net Gain, river, and ecological assessments were only 50% complete. Tender for development works (estimated £415,000) had not started, with August 2026 target.
findings.matters: Environmental constraints are delaying a £450k scheme and adding permit costs; suggests council capital delivery may face similar external blockers.
findings.figures: CCEME: £450,000 budget, £415,000 estimated development cost, £5,000 permit cost; £153 spent by 31 July
findings.quote: the calculated environmental risk score for the site is considered to be a HIGH and an environmental permit will be required.

findings.headline: Temporary Housing Scheme flagged RED and unlikely to complete in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Temporary Housing Scheme (TEMPH) is only 25% complete on both planned works. The Wellbrow property works were delayed because the property remained occupied, and are now rescheduled to 31 October 2026. Waddow Green level-access works have not started. Both milestones were originally due within the financial year.
findings.matters: Slippage in temporary accommodation provision directly affects the council's ability to meet homelessness obligations and suggests delivery constraints on housing schemes.
findings.figures: TEMPH: £21,500 budget, £0 spent, 0% committed as of 31 July
findings.quote: Works delayed as the property has been occupied

findings.headline: Council is purchasing affordable housing using S106 commuted sums and expanding its housing stock.
findings.detail: Three properties in Longridge were purchased using S106 monies to be resold as affordable housing. The scheme involved higher acquisition costs than budgeted, requiring release of additional S106 funds (£51,336 variance) to complete the purchases.
findings.matters: Shows active capital investment in housing stock and asset acquisition, using developer contributions as intended.
findings.figures: Three properties purchased in Longridge; S106 variance of £51,336
findings.quote: S106 monies were released to support the purchase of three properties in Longridge to be resold as Affordable Housing. These had not been included in the budget due to uncertainty over scheme details or timings.
